title: How to write a website redesign brief
description: A practical website redesign brief for founders and marketing teams: goals, page scope, content, integrations, migration, and handover.
author: The Wider Collective
takeaway: A useful redesign brief defines what visitors need to do, what your team needs to manage, and how you will judge the result. Start there before choosing a visual direction.

sections.heading: Start with the business decision
paragraphs: A website redesign is easier to scope when the brief describes a problem someone can observe. “Make it modern” leaves the agency guessing. “Help procurement teams find our capabilities and send a qualified enquiry” gives the project a direction.

Write down who visits the site, what they need to understand, and the action you want them to take. Separate primary audiences from occasional visitors. An investor, a job applicant, and a potential customer may need different routes through the same site.

Choose a small set of measures before work starts. Qualified enquiries, completed bookings, and the time your team spends updating content can all be useful. Establish a baseline where you have data; label an unmeasured assumption as an assumption.

sections.heading: Define pages, templates, and content
paragraphs: A page inventory and a template inventory answer different questions. Twenty service pages may share one layout. A calculator or searchable directory may require substantial work even if it occupies a single page. Ask proposals to describe both.

For each page, record its purpose, intended audience, content owner, and next action. Mark whether the copy and images exist, need editing, or must be created. Content production belongs in the schedule and budget.
Include language versions, forms, downloads, and accessibility requirements. If several people must approve the copy, name the person responsible for collecting their feedback.
bullets: Forms, search, calculators, and other interactive features
Required language versions and approval owners

sections.heading: Describe the operational requirements
paragraphs: Explain what your team needs to edit after launch: articles, staff profiles, services, case studies, or product information. Describe who will do it and how often. This helps the agency propose a content system that matches the work.

List the tools the website must connect to and the person who can provide access. Specify the expected behaviour of a lead form: where the enquiry arrives, who receives it, and what happens if delivery fails.

For an existing site, ask for a URL migration plan. Record valuable pages before changing addresses. Include redirects, metadata, sitemap checks, and verification that important content remains accessible.

sections.heading: Make remote delivery explicit
paragraphs: For an international project, agree on working-hour overlap, meeting frequency, and a single place for feedback. Record who can approve a milestone and what happens when feedback arrives after approval.

Ask which accounts, design files, code, and documentation you receive. Clarify hosting ownership, third-party subscriptions, training, support, and the process for later changes. These are practical questions to settle before comparing prices.

sections.heading: A brief you can copy
paragraphs: Use the prompts below to create a first draft. You do not need to solve every technical question before contacting an agency. A clearly labelled unknown is more useful than an invented requirement.

When proposals arrive, compare the same scope: strategy, copy, design, development, migration, testing, and support. Ask each team to identify exclusions and the decisions that could change the estimate.
bullets: Business problem: what is happening today?
Audience and action: who is the site for, and what should they do?
Scope: which pages, templates, languages, and features are required?
Content: what exists, who owns it, and what needs producing?
Operations: what must editors manage, and which tools must connect?
Delivery: budget parameters, target launch, decision-maker, and dependencies
Acceptance: how will we check the work and complete the handover?
